15:T33d3,<h2>Animating <code>width</code> triggers Layout, Paint, and Composite. Three stages, every frame. Animating <code>transform</code> triggers only Composite. One stage, on the GPU. Same visual result. Completely different cost.</h2>
<h2>The rendering waterfall</h2>
<p>The browser renders in stages. Each stage feeds the next. Triggering an early stage forces everything after it to re-run.</p>
<p><strong>Style → Layout → Paint → Composite</strong></p>
<p>Change <code>width</code>? The browser recalculates Layout, repaints pixels, re-composites layers. Three stages. On a page with 500 DOM nodes, that Layout step alone can take 10-50ms. Way over the 16ms budget for 60fps.</p>
<p>Change <code>color</code>? Layout stays the same. Repaint and re-composite. Two stages.</p>
<p>Change <code>transform</code>? Layout and Paint stay the same. Only re-composite. One stage. And it runs on the Compositor Thread, not the Main Thread. JavaScript can't block it. Heavy event handlers can't block it. Nothing on the Main Thread can touch it.</p>
<hr>
<h2>Which properties trigger what</h2>

























<table><thead><tr><th>Trigger</th><th>Properties</th><th>What happens</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Layout</td><td><code>width</code>, <code>height</code>, <code>margin</code>, <code>padding</code>, <code>top</code>, <code>left</code>, <code>font-size</code></td><td>Recalculates positions of surrounding elements. Expensive.</td></tr><tr><td>Paint</td><td><code>color</code>, <code>background</code>, <code>border-color</code>, <code>box-shadow</code>, <code>outline</code></td><td>Redraws pixels. Positions stay the same.</td></tr><tr><td>Composite</td><td><code>transform</code>, <code>opacity</code>, <code>filter</code></td><td>Re-composites layers on the GPU. Cheap.</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>For animations, always pick the Composite version:</p>





















<table><thead><tr><th>Instead of</th><th>Use</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>left</code> / <code>top</code> / <code>margin</code></td><td><code>transform: translateX/Y()</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>width</code> / <code>height</code></td><td><code>transform: scale()</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>display: none/block</code></td><td><code>opacity: 0/1</code></td></tr></tbody></table>
<hr>
<h2>Compositor layers</h2>
<p>Not every element gets its own layer. Each layer costs GPU memory. A 500x500 element takes roughly 1MB. The browser promotes elements to independent Compositor layers only when it has a reason to.</p>
<p><strong>What creates a layer:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>3D transforms.</strong> <code>translateZ(0)</code> and <code>translate3d()</code> trigger layer promotion immediately. 2D transforms like <code>translateX(50px)</code> usually don't, unless they're inside an active animation.</li>
<li><strong><code>will-change: transform</code>.</strong> Forces the browser to create a layer in advance. Use it on elements you know will animate. Remove it after. Keeping layers alive wastes memory.</li>
<li><strong><code>position: fixed</code>.</strong> Fixed elements get their own layer for smoother scrolling.</li>
<li><strong>Active CSS animations.</strong> Even 2D transforms temporarily get a layer during animation. The browser promotes them for the duration, then demotes them when it ends.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>What doesn't create a layer:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Hover states.</strong> Hover itself has nothing to do with layers. A <code>color</code> change on hover stays on the Main Thread. Only the animation <em>triggered by</em> hover might create one.</li>
<li><strong>Static <code>transform</code>.</strong> <code>transform: translateX(50px)</code> without animation or <code>will-change</code> is just a layout hint. No layer promotion.</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h2>What this looks like in practice</h2>
<p>A sidebar that slides in. Two ways to build it.</p>

Animating `width` triggers Layout, Paint, and Composite. Three stages, every frame. Animating `transform` triggers only Composite. One stage, on the GPU. Same visual result. Completely different cost.
---

## The rendering waterfall

The browser renders in stages. Each stage feeds the next. Triggering an early stage forces everything after it to re-run.

**Style → Layout → Paint → Composite**

Change `width`? The browser recalculates Layout, repaints pixels, re-composites layers. Three stages. On a page with 500 DOM nodes, that Layout step alone can take 10-50ms. Way over the 16ms budget for 60fps.

Change `color`? Layout stays the same. Repaint and re-composite. Two stages.

Change `transform`? Layout and Paint stay the same. Only re-composite. One stage. And it runs on the Compositor Thread, not the Main Thread. JavaScript can't block it. Heavy event handlers can't block it. Nothing on the Main Thread can touch it.

---

## Which properties trigger what

| Trigger | Properties | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Layout | `width`, `height`, `margin`, `padding`, `top`, `left`, `font-size` | Recalculates positions of surrounding elements. Expensive. |
| Paint | `color`, `background`, `border-color`, `box-shadow`, `outline` | Redraws pixels. Positions stay the same. |
| Composite | `transform`, `opacity`, `filter` | Re-composites layers on the GPU. Cheap. |

For animations, always pick the Composite version:

| Instead of | Use |
|---|---|
| `left` / `top` / `margin` | `transform: translateX/Y()` |
| `width` / `height` | `transform: scale()` |
| `display: none/block` | `opacity: 0/1` |

---

## Compositor layers

Not every element gets its own layer. Each layer costs GPU memory. A 500x500 element takes roughly 1MB. The browser promotes elements to independent Compositor layers only when it has a reason to.

**What creates a layer:**

- **3D transforms.** `translateZ(0)` and `translate3d()` trigger layer promotion immediately. 2D transforms like `translateX(50px)` usually don't, unless they're inside an active animation.
- **`will-change: transform`.** Forces the browser to create a layer in advance. Use it on elements you know will animate. Remove it after. Keeping layers alive wastes memory.
- **`position: fixed`.** Fixed elements get their own layer for smoother scrolling.
- **Active CSS animations.** Even 2D transforms temporarily get a layer during animation. The browser promotes them for the duration, then demotes them when it ends.

**What doesn't create a layer:**

- **Hover states.** Hover itself has nothing to do with layers. A `color` change on hover stays on the Main Thread. Only the animation *triggered by* hover might create one.
- **Static `transform`.** `transform: translateX(50px)` without animation or `will-change` is just a layout hint. No layer promotion.

---

## What this looks like in practice

A sidebar that slides in. Two ways to build it.

```css
/* Animating width: Layout reflow every frame */
.sidebar {
  width: 0;
  transition: width 0.3s;
}
.sidebar.open {
  width: 240px;
}
```

DevTools shows: Layout (12ms) → Paint (3ms) → Composite (0.5ms). Every frame. On a page with a data table, those Layout events cascade. The table recalculates column widths, rows reflow, the whole page shifts. Total frame time: 40ms. That's 25fps. Users see jank.

```css
/* Animating transform: Compositor only */
.sidebar {
  width: 240px;
  transform: translateX(-100%);
  transition: transform 0.3s;
}
.sidebar.open {
  transform: translateX(0);
}
```

DevTools shows: Composite (0.5ms). That's it. The sidebar has its own layer during the transition. The Main Thread never gets involved. 60fps on a budget Android phone.

The sidebar is always 240px wide. It just starts off-screen and slides in. Same visual result. No reflow.

---

## The `will-change` trap

Developers discovered `will-change` and slapped it on everything.

```css
/* Don't do this */
* { will-change: transform, opacity; }
```

Each `will-change` creates a layer. Each layer costs memory. A page with 200 elements promoted to layers can eat 200MB of GPU memory. On mobile, the browser runs out and starts thrashing. The "optimization" makes things worse.

Use `will-change` like a scalpel:

```css
/* Add it right before animation */
.card:hover {
  will-change: transform;
}
.card:active {
  transform: scale(0.98);
  transition: transform 0.1s;
}
```

Or better: let CSS animations handle it. The browser auto-promotes elements during `transition` and `animation`. You only need `will-change` when you want the layer created *before* the animation starts, to avoid a first-frame hitch.

---

## Quick checklist

1. **Animate only `transform` and `opacity`.** These are the only properties guaranteed to run on the Compositor Thread.
2. **Use `will-change` on one or two elements, not globally.** Remove it after animation ends.
3. **Open DevTools Performance tab.** If you see green "Paint" bars during animation, you're not on the Compositor Thread.
4. **Test on real devices.** Compositor animations look the same everywhere. Layout animations fall apart on slow hardware.
